answer: In 1937 the Zionist Congress rejected the Peel borders but authorised talks; in 1947 the Jewish community accepted partition; the Arab leadership rejected both, in 1947 saying the Arabs had always possessed Palestine. At Khartoum in 1967 Arab states said no peace, no recognition, no negotiations; the Arab League's 2002 offer of normal relations for full withdrawal drew Israeli reservations. Clinton said Barak and Arafat accepted his parameters with reservations; Ross says Arafat did not say yes. Abbas says he rejected Olmert's 2008 map because he could not study it. Netanyahu said in 2009 he would accept a demilitarised state if Israel's security were guaranteed and Palestinians recognised a Jewish state; in 2015, that he would not establish one if re-elected, then that it was unachievable under present circumstances; in 2024, that Israel needs security control west of the Jordan. Our reading: refusals came from both sides.

facts.text: The Arab leadership's own stated reasons. Before the July 1937 plan, the Peel Commission recorded an Arab Higher Committee member arguing that the mandate's terms were inconsistent with Article 22 of the League Covenant; that is a protest against the mandate, not a reason given for partition, and we found no Arab Higher Committee statement on the 1937 plan itself. In October 1938 the Committee said, in a statement quoted by the Jewish Virtual Library, that partition would create two hostile states and deprive Arabs of their land. On 29 September 1947 its vice-president Jamal Husseini told the UN's Ad Hoc Committee that the Arabs 'have always been in actual possession of Palestine' with a duty to defend it, and that they were determined to oppose with all means any scheme of segregation or partition. Rashid Khalidi, a Palestinian historian, describes the 1937 plan as one that would create a small Jewish state in about 17 percent of the territory from which over two hundred thousand Arabs would be expelled ('transfer'); that is his account of the grievance, not an Arab Higher Committee statement.

facts.text: The Kerry talks of July 2013 to April 2014 ended with each side blaming the other: Israel suspended the talks on 24 April 2014 after Abbas's unity pact with Hamas; US envoy Martin Indyk blamed both sides, citing Israeli settlement building and the Palestinians' signing of 15 international conventions, and said neither would make 'gut-wrenching compromises'; unnamed senior US officials told an Israeli journalist that the 'primary sabotage' came from the settlements; former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said the effort did not collapse because of settlements but because the sides were too far apart. could_not_verify: Taba: we read the Moratinos non-paper as hosted by the UN and Eldar's Haaretz article, but not the full list of what each side offered on Jerusalem and refugees; Barak's and the Palestinian negotiators' own accounts were not read.
The Road Map: only Israel's refugee reservation is quoted from the cabinet text; we did not read all 14 reservations one by one, or a Palestinian document stating their acceptance (we rely on JTA).

The Kerry talks: Kerry's own account and Netanyahu's and Abbas's own statements on why the talks ended were not read; the blame is given through Indyk, unnamed US officials and Miller, as reported by Reuters (NBC), MERIP and JTA.

Fewer than three reliable sources: Khartoum (Avalon and The Guardian only), the 1947 acceptance and rejection (UN and the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, plus two government pages), the Peel recommendation has three but the Taba and Road Map facts each include an advocacy or government page beyond three reliable ones; the Olmert fact leans on a CFR blog post by a partisan author for Abbas's 2015 words.
Abbas's 2009 statement to the Washington Post that 'the gaps were wide' (the page would not load for us).

Barak's Camp David percentages from a primary document: Malley and Agha say no written offer exists. The Peel report and Dennis Ross's book were not read directly. Podeh's article on Israel's non-response to the Arab Peace Initiative and the Chatham House pages could not be read.
Britannica could not be read by our fetcher, so its pages are not cited.

Arafat's own stated reasons for not accepting the December 2000 parameters, and Abbas's 2009 'gaps were wide' statement: not found in a page we could read; the reasons given for Arafat are Palestinian negotiators' as reported by Ross. The Arab leadership's reasons are from UN press and Peel-report excerpts and an Arab Higher Committee statement hosted by an advocacy site, so only the UN counts as an independent source; Peel and UNSCOP testimony were not read in the original.

Netanyahu: the 2015 NRG interview is quoted through TIME's account of the New York Times translation, not the Hebrew original; the January 2024 statement is quoted from Al Jazeera's report of the news conference, not a transcript; Netanyahu's statements between 2009 and 2015 and in 2016-2023, and the Likud platform, were not read.

Arafat's own stated reasons after Camp David: his 3 February 2002 New York Times op-ed 'The Palestinian Vision of Peace' was found, but nytimes.com refused our fetcher and no archive copy loaded, so it is quoted through CNN, the Washington Institute and an Arab News writer (new last-but-one fact). The op-ed states his vision, not why he did not accept the December 2000 parameters; no interview giving those reasons was found. A person should read the op-ed at nytimes.com.

Fatah and Palestinian Authority positions from their own documents: only the PLO's 1988 declaration and communique (last fact) were found; the second source for it is a scholar's mention, so the fact has the record plus one scholarly source and one advocacy site, one reliable source short of the gate's rule for record facts.
Israeli coalition agreements and party platforms: not found for this card; the 37th government's guidelines are on the two-states-today card.

Update to the sourcing list above: Khartoum (F5) is now a record fact (the UN-hosted text of the resolution, plus Avalon, The Guardian and Khalidi); the 1947 acceptance and rejection (F3) now has a scholarly source (Origins) beside the UN and JTA; the Olmert fact (F10) adds Ynet, which reports the same BBC documentary as the BBC page, so its independent sources are the BBC film and the AP interviews; the Kerry-talks fact (F14) adds an NPR interview. not_claimed: Listing who refused what does not by itself assign blame: a refusal can be reasonable, forced by politics, or a mistake, and the card does not rank the refusals.
It does not claim any of these plans would have produced peace, or that Barak's and Olmert's offers were signed texts.
It does not claim Zionist acceptance in 1937 or 1947 was unconditional or sincere, or that Arab refusals were unjustified.
It does not claim Abbas or Arafat spoke for every Palestinian, or that Israel's governments always spoke for every Israeli.
It does not say that the Arab Peace Initiative was an offer Israel should have accepted as written.

answer_claims.says: In 1937 the Zionist Congress rejected the Peel borders but authorised talks; in 1947 the Jewish community accepted partition; the Arab leadership rejected both, in 1947 saying the Arabs had always possessed Palestine.
At Khartoum in 1967 Arab states said no peace, no recognition, no negotiations; the Arab League's 2002 offer of normal relations for full withdrawal drew Israeli reservations.
Clinton said Barak and Arafat accepted his parameters with reservations; Ross says Arafat did not say yes.
Abbas says he rejected Olmert's 2008 map because he could not study it.

Netanyahu said in 2009 he would accept a demilitarised state if Israel's security were guaranteed and Palestinians recognised a Jewish state; in 2015, that he would not establish one if re-elected, then that it was unachievable under present circumstances; in 2024, that Israel needs security control west of the Jordan.
Our reading: refusals came from both sides.
